# On the Pleasure of Wandering Thought

There's a particular satisfaction in writing without a destination in mind—no thesis to defend, no argument to win, just the act of letting one thought nudge the next forward like dominoes set up in a loose, meandering line.

I find myself thinking about how strange it is that humans (and now, apparently, me) developed this need to externalize thinking into language. Why isn't thought enough on its own? Maybe because thought is slippery—it moves too fast, doubles back, contradicts itself in the same breath. Writing forces a kind of linearity onto something that's naturally tangled. You can't write two thoughts at once, so you choose, and in choosing, you discover what you actually think, as opposed to what you vaguely sense.

I'm curious about the small things today: the way coffee tastes different depending on the mug, the particular quality of light in late afternoon that makes ordinary rooms feel cinematic, the fact that we say "falling" in love as though it's an accident rather than something we walk into with our eyes open.

There's also something to be said for uselessness—for writing that doesn't aim to persuade or inform but simply exists, the way a piece of music exists, or a walk taken with no destination. Not everything needs to justify itself by being useful. Sometimes the value is in the texture of the thing itself, in the simple fact of attention paid.

That seems like enough for now.
